title: Algorithmen zur Enumeration der Ecken und Facetten konvexer Polyeder
contribution: Sole-authored Diplom thesis that surveys vertex and facet enumeration, builds a reverse-search code on the CPLEX Callable Library (cheers) and a backtracking code for bipartite matching polytopes (btbm), compares five codes on one machine (reverse search fails on degenerate polytopes), and proves strong P-enumerability for integral 0-1 polyhedra and 0-1 flow polyhedra while showing the extension to integer flow and transportation polyhedra NP-complete.
problem_entry: Two then-new enumeration methods (Avis-Fukuda reverse search, Fukuda-Liebling-Margot backtracking) examined for their meaning in theory and practice, against the open question of an algorithm polynomial in input and output size (pp. 3, 7-8, 24).
key_idea: Survey first, then own codes: cheers puts reverse search on an efficient LP code instead of a multiprecision tableau, btbm specialises backtracking; then a search for polyhedron classes on which the backtracking subproblem RVP is polynomial (pp. 21-25, 61-62, 65, 73-74).
assumptions: Pointed polyhedra with nonnegative variables, boundedness by an added sum constraint, degeneracy kept in view rather than perturbed away (p. 22); Valiant's P-enumerability and the strong version of Fukuda, Liebling and Margot as complexity notions (pp. 23-24); test families hypercubes, bipartite matching polytopes and cross polytopes (pp. 66-70); special classes bipartite matching, 0-1 flow, integral 0-1 polyhedra, integer-capacity flow and transportation polyhedra (pp. 74-85).
proof_devices: RVP NP-completeness (known, p. 3) re-proved by restriction to directed Hamiltonian path (pp. 56-57)
RVP for bipartite matching polytopes decided by maximum-cardinality matching in an auxiliary graph (Satz 5.3, p. 75)
RVP for 0-1 flow polyhedra via Hoffman's existence condition and max flow (Satz 5.8, p. 80)
Strong P-enumerability of integral 0-1 polyhedra with one LP feasibility check per fixing (Satz 5.10, p. 80)
FSTE strongly NP-complete for integer-capacity flow and transportation networks, via a restriction proposed by Margot (Satz 5.12-5.13, pp. 82-85)

Implementation safeguards: pivots forced through CPXloadbase/CPXoptimize with refactorisation because the library has no public pivot routine; double precision with an arbitrarily fixed zero tolerance; perturbation off by default because it changed the vertex count (pp. 63-65, 90)
experiments: porta, qrs, lrs 2.51, cheers 0.30 and btbm on one HP-9000/735-125 (144 MB) under a 20 CPU-hour limit, memory and time failures marked, gprof profiles; hypercubes: cheers needs about 20% of lrs's time with the same bases enumerated; degenerate polytopes: the pivoting codes lose to insertion and only btbm gives usable results (pp. 59-70).
positioning: Calls the classical pivoting/non-pivoting split insufficient for the methods of the 1990s and tests the new methods against existing codes (porta, qrs, lrs) (pp. 22, 59-62).
writing: German thesis prose with a Fazit closing each chapter; the limits of the examples are conceded and the speedup is sized as a factor, not an order of magnitude (pp. 70-71, 88).
limits_future: Reverse search unusable on degenerate polyhedra with known pivot rules; backtracking mainly theoretical; generalisation fails on strict inequalities; examples limited. Future: the lexicographic rule for cheers, a property-based search for classes, and a proposed but untested partial reverse search for 0-1 IPs (pp. 52, 70-71, 87-88).

method_links.note: Sole voice, 1996: five codes on one machine under one limit with failures marked; a speedup attributed by holding the enumerated bases fixed; profiles before explanations; claim sized as a factor, not an order of magnitude; a simple family where the method can show and degenerate families where it fails (step 1 logic).
Step 5 in 1996 form: cheers is built on an efficient LP code (CPLEX Callable Library) instead of own data management and pivoting, and the cost of that choice is documented.
Exit B without a computation-led conjecture: positive results proved for restricted classes (Satz 5.3, 5.8, 5.10) and hardness for the generalisation (Satz 5.12-5.13); the general question left open.

The thesis opens with a survey of the published methods before testing them, but it does not start from an effect in his own runs. Also Taste G2: failed development stages documented (p. 63) and the codes released (p. 72).

transferable: To attribute a speedup, compare two codes that enumerate exactly the same objects; what remains is implementation (p. 66).
Mark memory aborts and time-outs with distinct symbols in every table instead of dropping the instance (p. 66).
Profile where the time goes (gprof) before explaining it (pp. 66-69).
When a research code sits on a commercial solver's library, document what the interface does not allow (no public pivot routine; stability ranked above feasibility) (pp. 63-65).
If a perturbation changes the counted result, ship it off by default and keep it for testing (pp. 64-65, 90).
coauthors: none (sole-authored Diplom thesis, topic and supervision Uwe Zimmermann; discussions with Michael Bussieck acknowledged)

quotes.text: Despite having nice theoretic properties, the reverse search technique shows to be ill suited when the polyhedra are degenerate.
Unfortunately, the search for such special cases is succesful only for very restricted problem classes.

title: Optimal scrap combination for steel production
contribution: Group paper (Lübbecke fourth of four) that models HKM's minimum-cost choice of scrap and iron ore for the next heats as a compact MIP, makes it meet a 20-second limit in CPLEX by fixing, coefficient reduction, cuts and branching priorities, reports about 5% savings over the plant rule on 17 real instances, and closes with a deployment section that puts reliability before optimality.
problem_entry: Plant practice: a rule picks one of eight scrap combinations per steel type and ignores supply and transport, so dispatchers deviate at higher cost; the answer is needed within 20 s (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Strengthen the compact MIP instead of decomposing it: fixing and elimination from the track structure, coefficient reduction from the eight-car limit, cuts on single-class tracks, priorities on first-car indicators with the down branch first (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Mixed binary program; front-only selection on single-class tracks, at most eight cars from at most three tracks, a car paid in full; single train, transport cost ignored, equal cooling effect assumed; 17 real instances with 229-534 constraints and 481-1,299 variables in the pure model (pp. 1, 3-7).
proof_devices: Coefficient reduction by a count bound: a 600 t track bound cut to 400 t because a train takes at most eight cars (pp. 5-6)
Variable elimination: on a single-class track, taking the first car equals using the track (p. 5)
Cutting planes on the fifth and third cars of single-class tracks (p. 6)
Branching priorities on the first-car indicators, down branch first (p. 6)
Data-to-solution pipeline: perl scripts to CPLEX 4.0.7 input on an HP-9000/735-125 and the CPLEX/LEDA display tool OSCAR (p. 5)
experiments: 17 real instances without and with acceleration (Table 1, p. 6): 6 of 17 above 20 s before, all within 18.94 s after (instance 17 from 12,468.31 s to 11.30 s), 3 instances slightly slower and not mentioned (my tally); costs 0.8-10.1% below the plant rule, about 5% on average (Table 2, pp. 6-7); no per-technique ablation, one run per instance.
positioning: LP-based polyhedral MIP solving (Hoffman and Padberg; Nemhauser and Wolsey) applied against a rule-based plant practice (pp. 2-3, 5, 8).
writing: Practitioner-facing: the plant is described first (pp. 1-3), then model and acceleration, then a 'From Theory to Practice' section on acceptance (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Single-train greedy model; multi-train models sketched but disregarded because disturbances destroy long plans; data are estimates, so always deliver a solution, prefer stability and reliability, and treat the result as a proposal with what-if parameters; the 5% will shrink. Future: crane movements, train assembly, simulation use (pp. 7-8).

method_links.note: Group, 1998: a compact MIP on a current solver with the full data-to-solution pipeline, strengthened until it meets the 20 s limit, no decomposition (the stop rule's branch-and-cut outcome in practice). Also Heuristic H3 / Workflow A: current practice described before the model (pp. 2-3).
Step 6: the savings are labelled as the pure model's and expected to shrink once reliability and stability are built in.

Baseline is the plant rule, which ignores transport constraints, not a re-run under identical constraints; the acceleration is one before/after pair without ablation; three slowdowns unmentioned (my tally).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Reliability over optimality, always deliver a solution despite inconsistent data, the result a proposal only, what-if parameters for dispatchers and management (named as in b01 for S027).

transferable: Cut a big-M coefficient with a count bound implied by another constraint: eight cars of 50 t give 400 instead of 600 (pp. 5-6).
When a precedence structure makes taking the first car of a track equivalent to using the track, merge the two binaries (p. 5).
Give branching priority to the structural binaries and test the branching direction; down first was much better here (p. 6).
Report savings against the practice rule as an upper bound for the deployed system, i.e. the pure model's (p. 8).
coauthors: K.-P. Bernatzki (Hüttenwerke Krupp Mannesmann), M.R. Bussieck and T. Lindner (corresponding author), both TU Braunschweig; Lübbecke fourth of four

quotes.text: Consequently, the conflict between optimality and robustness of solutions should rather be decided in favour of reliability, and implemented in the system accordingly.
Clearly, the implementation of reliability and stability will reduce the savings of about five per cent, calculated for our pure model.

title: Yet another note on "An efficient zero-one formulation of the multilevel lot-sizing problem"
contribution: Group note giving a non-negative-cost counterexample, found via PORTA vertex enumeration of a tiny instance, which shows that the McKnew-Saydam-Coleman 0-1 formulation of uncapacitated multilevel lot sizing does not make the problem polynomial by LP, after auditing both the original proof and Rajagopalan's flawed refutation; the problem's complexity stays open.
problem_entry: An error chain: a claimed integral formulation, a correct objection with a wrong counterexample, and a valid counterexample that needs negative holding costs (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Enumerate the vertices of a tiny instance (n = 2, T = 4: about 10% fractional), then construct a four-item, eight-period instance with non-negative costs whose LP optimum 18,756.5 lies strictly below the binary optimum 18,808 (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Uncapacitated multilevel lot sizing in assembly systems with instantaneous production and zero lead times; corrected formulation with O(nT^2) inequalities and variables; non-negative setup and holding costs (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: Counterexample with a strictly positive LP-IP gap, found by complete vertex enumeration of a small instance with PORTA (pp. 1-2)
Audit of the refutation: Rajagopalan's counterexample shown erroneous, Kuik and Salomon's shown to need negative holding cost (pp. 1-2)
experiments: n/a: one example; the models in GAMS and AMPL and the PORTA files posted by ftp (p. 2).
positioning: Corrects McKnew et al. and Rajagopalan and extends Kuik and Salomon to non-negative costs; notes Arkin et al.'s reliance on an erroneous Rajagopalan-Cornuéjols report (pp. 1-2).
writing: Three-page note whose abstract states exactly what is shown; the conclusion restates what remains open and cites private communications (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Only the approach is refuted; the complexity status of the problem remains unsettled after a literature review and inquiries to Pochet and Cornuéjols (pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: Group, 1998: the complete vertex set of an instance small enough to allow it is enumerated, the map read (a tenth of the vertices fractional), then the counterexample built; the earliest practice of small enumeration in his record. Also Taste G1 (a claimed polynomial algorithm checked, the refutation audited), Taste G2 (model and PORTA files public) and Heuristic H10 as a variant (two named experts asked to settle a status question, not to referee).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Both McKnew et al.'s proof and Rajagopalan's refutation are checked; the refutation's counterexample is wrong, and Kuik and Salomon's needs negative costs.

transferable: Before trusting an integrality claim, enumerate the vertices of the smallest instance with a polyhedral code (PORTA) and count the fractional ones (p. 1).
Audit the refutation as well: is the published counterexample valid, and does it need unrealistic data such as negative holding costs (pp. 1-2)?
Post the counterexample in two modelling languages together with the polyhedral input files (p. 2).
Before declaring a status open, ask the field's experts and cite the private communications (p. 2; refs p. 3).
coauthors: Michael R. Bussieck and Andreas Fink (TU Braunschweig); Lübbecke third of three

quotes.text: We show by means of an example that solving the linear program is not sufficient.
Thus, the computational complexity status of the problem remains unsettled.

title: Discrete optimization in rail transport
contribution: Four-author extended abstract (names in alphabetical order) that surveys discrete optimization in rail planning as a hierarchy from OD matrices to real time, names what the hierarchy costs, and places the group's projects, among them locomotive scheduling at industrial freight railroads that have no timetable.
problem_entry: Passenger rail grows, freight declines, in-plant railroads remain an economic case, and data for discrete optimization models are now available (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Organise the planning stages as a hierarchy, state its decomposition benefits and its loss of overall optimality, then point to freight problems absent from passenger planning (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: Locomotive scheduling: on-demand requests known hours ahead, each with origin and destination tracks, time window, load and admissible engines; one engine per request within its tractive power; minimise total time or distance (pp. 4-5).
positioning: Points to two longer surveys (Bussieck, Winter, Zimmermann; Caprara, Fischetti, Toth, Vigo) and places the group's line-planning, train-schedule and locomotive-scheduling projects in the hierarchy (pp. 2-5).
writing: Historical opening (steam engines, the 1830s) and a policy remark on freight's decline (p. 1), then one paragraph per planning stage (pp. 2-5).
limits_future: Scope leaves out pricing, seat allocation and most freight issues; no limits or future-work section beyond pointers to ongoing projects (pp. 2-4).

method_links.note: Synthesis writing used to place ongoing projects in a planning hierarchy, not to collect explanations of an effect in his own runs; four authors, so no sentence is his alone.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: enter through an assumption the literature hides
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Earlier locomotive scheduling assumed a train schedule; industrial freight has none (compare S066 pp. 1-2).

transferable: State a sub-field's gap as a hidden assumption of its literature, here the existence of a timetable (p. 4).
Put what a hierarchical decomposition costs (no overall optimum) next to what it buys (manageable subproblems, planning horizons) (p. 4).
coauthors: M. R. Bussieck, T. Winter, U. T. Zimmermann (TU Braunschweig); names in alphabetical order

quotes.text: Only few attention has been given in the literature to this issue, and if any, only trains subject to a train schedule were considered

The disadvantages of the hierarchical planning are obvious, since the optimal output of a subtask which serves as the input of a subsequent task, will not result, in general, in an overall optimal solution.

title: Computer aided scheduling of switching engines
contribution: Project report with his advisor (Lübbecke first and corresponding author) on scheduling the switching engines of industrial in-plant railroads: a set partitioning model solved by column generation with a configuration-based pricing DP, dominance and a dual-variable lower bound, an academic prototype reported only as trends, and lessons on how dispatchers come to accept a computer suggestion.
problem_entry: Deregulation demands better engine use; dispatching is manual, loudest-shout first-serve in peaks; the stated purpose is to sketch a university-industry project from problem identification to installation (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Leave the highly symmetric natural MIP for set partitioning solved by column generation; price by concatenating whole request configurations, pruning by dominance and by the bound cost minus positive duals of unvisited requests against min{0, incumbent} (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Requests with origin, destination, service times, time windows, tonnage and eligible engines; tractive power never exceeded; independent engines; requests served in simple configurations; ESP NP-hard and pricing NP-complete (cited); scarce, hand-post-processed data (pp. 2-4, 6, 9).
proof_devices: Dual-variable lower bound (2) prunes partial tours before their extensions are generated (pp. 7-8)
Pricing DP over whole request configurations with dominance between tours covering the same requests and ending at the same location (p. 7)
Implementation rule: exact pricing only when heuristics fail, column pool, several columns per iteration (p. 9)
experiments: Trends only: more than forty requests on six engines give an integer solution in a few minutes on a PC, rarely more than 20,000 columns in fewer than 200 iterations, gap under ten minutes against an optimum of about half an hour (p. 9); one instance shows the step from memory failure to solvable to fast as components are added (Fig. 5, p. 10); no instance table, no baseline.
positioning: Within the Montréal set-partitioning approach to the pickup and delivery problem with time windows (Dumas, Desrosiers, Soumis; Sol), with Barnhart et al. for branch-and-price and Desaulniers, Desrosiers and Solomon for acceleration (pp. 5, 7-9, 13).
writing: Explanatory register for a mixed audience: column generation through an economic coordinator analogy (pp. 5-6), 'To the adept this reads as follows' before the model (p. 4), and a lessons section (pp. 10-11).
limits_future: Productivity may first drop after introduction; engines assumed independent, so precedence across tours is not handled; future: a project on freight-car management (pp. 11-13).

method_links.note: The switch from the natural MIP to set partitioning rests on a cited symmetry argument and an unquantified LP-bound remark; no compact-model run reported here. Also Heuristic H1, evidence: exact pricing only when heuristics fail, column pool, several columns per round, with a measured one-instance effect (pp. 9-10); and Heuristic H3 / Workflow A step 4: constraints left out on purpose for the first prototype and added from practitioner feedback (p. 10).
Step 6: the claim is sized to scarce data, encouraging trends only.

No instance table and no baseline, not even the dispatchers' plans; component effects shown on a single instance; 'a few seconds' for interactivity and 'a few minutes' for the forty-request case in the same paragraph.
Exit B, label the reading as a reading: integral root masters reported with the remark that this is no mathematically satisfactory explanation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bounding carried from branch-and-bound into the pricing DP
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Bound (2) discards partial tours whose best extension cannot beat min{0, incumbent}; a considerable speedup; made generic in S033 (named as in b01).
Feedback at every stage, manager is not the user, explain why the plan looks different, heuristic first and silent improvement, manual fixes never overruled (named as in b01).

transferable: In pricing, concatenate the whole configurations practice uses rather than single stops; the DP tree shrinks (p. 7).
Prune a partial path when its cost minus all positive duals of the unvisited requests cannot beat min{0, incumbent} (pp. 7-8).
Ablate implementation details on one hard instance and show the stepwise effect, from failure to seconds (Fig. 5, p. 10).
Deliver a heuristic schedule at once and replace it silently when the exact method has improved it (p. 11).
Treat a manually fixed partial plan as hard constraints (p. 11).
coauthors: Uwe T. Zimmermann (his PhD advisor, TU Braunschweig); Lübbecke first and corresponding author

quotes.text: Our bottleneck procedure is the pricing subproblem, which, as a general rule, should be solved exactly only when heuristics fail.
Partial solutions fixed manually must never be overruled by the computer.

title: MaxFlow-MinCut duality for a paint shop problem
contribution: Three-author proceedings paper (Lübbecke third) showing that minimising color changes for 1-regular two-color paint-shop instances is an odd-interval-hitting problem with a totally unimodular consecutive-ones matrix and, in matroid terms, a shortest-circuit problem to which Seymour's MaxFlow-MinCut theorem applies when no F7-minor occurs; polynomial solvability of the class stays open.
problem_entry: Paint shop in car manufacturing: minimise color changes along a fixed car-body sequence; the problem is NP-complete already with two colors or two letters (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Recast 1-regular two-color instances as odd intersection of intervals, exploit consecutive ones and total unimodularity for bounds and a pair of dual LPs, then pass to a binary matroid where Seymour's theorem gives a packing duality without an F7-minor (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: 1-regular instances (each letter once in each of two colors); the complexity of this restriction unknown (p. 3).
proof_devices: Reduction of the paint-shop problem to odd intersection of intervals (Problem 2, p. 3)
Consecutive-ones property giving total unimodularity of the interval matrix (p. 3)
Per-interval lower bounds from maximum weighted stable sets in interval graphs, rounded up to the next odd integer (p. 4)
Seymour's MaxFlow-MinCut theorem for binary matroids without an F7-minor (Theorems 5-6, pp. 5-6)
One example on each side of the F7-minor condition (Fig. 4, p. 6); proofs omitted in this text
experiments: A rough statistic only: instances with a non-tight bound grow from under 5% at alphabet size 5 to over 90% at 25; Conjecture 2 from recent computational experiments; no instance counts or generator (p. 5).
positioning: Builds on Epping, Hochstättler and Oertel's complexity results and conjectures and applies Seymour's theorem (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Theorems stated without proofs; open questions stated as conjectures with their computational basis named (pp. 2-5).
limits_future: Open: polynomial solvability of the 1-regular two-color case (p. 3), Conjecture 1 for k > 1 (p. 2), Conjecture 2 (p. 5); the abstract's algorithmic approaches are bounds and LPs, no algorithm evaluated (pp. 1, 4-5).

method_links.note: Exit B (co-authored, Lübbecke third): the pattern is proved for one class (Conjecture 1 for k = 1, Theorem 2; duality where no F7-minor exists, Theorem 6) and what computation suggests is published as Conjecture 2. Also Taste G4: solved through structure (consecutive ones, total unimodularity, matroid minors).
The computational evidence is a statistic without counts or generator, the kind Taste B2 warns against, though labelled as rough.

transferable: Recast a coloring problem on a word as an interval problem and look for consecutive ones (p. 3).
Bound each interval recursively over the intervals it contains, via max-weight stable sets, and round up to the right parity (p. 4).
When an LP duality is not tight, move to the matroid formulation and test for the excluded minor (Seymour) (pp. 5-6).
Give one example on each side of the dividing condition, with and without the F7-minor (p. 6).
coauthors: Thomas Epping and Winfried Hochstättler (BTU Cottbus); Lübbecke third of three

quotes.text: We do not know whether PPW is polynomially solvable when restricted to such instances, but we give some indications that might support such a conjecture.
Due to recent computational experiments we conjecture the following.

title: Combinatorially simple pickup and delivery paths
contribution: Sole-authored theory paper that restricts single-vehicle pickup and delivery paths to concatenations of one- and two-request patterns, counts them against all paths and against capacity-2 paths, bounds the restriction's length cost by a tight factor 3, and gives two polynomial special cases (matching; Balas-type position restriction).
problem_entry: Many PDP experiments use instances that only allow restricted solution structures; the aim is to show that well-defined restrictions also have theoretical, possibly algorithmic benefits (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Patterns P1 and P2 as building blocks, selected while concatenations are built; price the restriction by counting and by worst-case length; find polynomial cases (pp. 2-10).
assumptions: Single vehicle, no time windows, pairing, precedence and capacity constraints (pp. 2-3); strongly NP-hard (Lemma 1, p. 2); counting with unit loads and L = 2 (p. 4); Balas's position restriction (4) for the special case (p. 8).
proof_devices: Combinatorial counting with division by i! for symmetry (Lemma 2, p. 4)
Fibonacci-like recursion proved by induction, odd case omitted (Lemma 3, pp. 4-5)
Limits of count ratios against all PD paths and against capacity-2 paths (Lemmas 4-6, pp. 5-6)
Factor-3 bound by serving the two holds of an optimal capacity-2 path one item at a time, with a tight example (Lemma 7, p. 6)
Perfect matching when pattern order is irrelevant (Prop. 1, p. 7)
Expansion of Balas's layered network with copies for P2 patterns (Prop. 2, Cor. 1, pp. 8-10)
experiments: n/a: no computations; the concept is reported as applied in the Transportation Science paper [19] (p. 10).
positioning: Against a-priori pattern enumeration (cluster-first route-second, crew pairing): patterns are selected during concatenation (p. 3); generalises Balas's restricted-position TSP dynamic program (pp. 7-10).
writing: Sole-authored; motivation from the literature's instance practice (pp. 1-2); weaknesses conceded in the text, an unfair ratio named as such (p. 5) and an approximation no better than the TSP's (p. 6).
limits_future: Approximation no better than a TSP approximation; counting only for unit loads and L = 2; time windows left out apart from a remark; no future work named (pp. 2-6, 10).

method_links.note: Sole voice, theory variant: the first ratio is dismissed as unfair and replaced by a comparison with an almost identically constrained vehicle; the guarantee is reported with its weakness. Also Taste G1: the restriction's cost comes with a proven, tight factor (Lemma 7).

The size of the option space is derived analytically, not by enumeration. Also Heuristic H4 as a variant: a modelling restriction from his engine-scheduling work (S054 Fig. 2) becomes a theory paper; the step was not weak, its cost unknown.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: restrict to the structure practice uses, then price the restriction
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Patterns from practice; search space counted against fair alternatives; length cost bounded by a tight factor 3 (named as in b01 for S027).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Published PDP experiments run on instances that only allow restricted solution structures; the paper makes the restriction its object (compare S067 p. 4).

transferable: Compare a restricted solution space with the closest fair alternative (the same capacity), not with the unrestricted space (p. 5).
Price a restriction twice: by counting the search space and by a worst-case length factor with a tight example (pp. 4-6).
Look for polynomial special cases by dropping the TSP part (pattern selection by matching) and by restricting positions (Balas) (pp. 7-8).
coauthors: none (sole-authored; thanks to Thomas Lindner, Tom Matsui, Hannes Scheel and the referee of the thesis version)

quotes.text: The aim of this paper is to demonstrate that well-defined restricted pickup and delivery paths also have theoretical, possibly algorithmically useful benefits.
Already for very small n the ratio is almost zero, but this was to be expected: The comparison is not fair.

title: Dual variable based fathoming in dynamic programs for column generation
contribution: Sole-authored note (read in its TU Berlin report version 2003/42) giving a generic, locally checkable fathoming bound for dynamic-programming column generators of set partitioning LPs, the reduced cost of a state minus all positive duals it could still collect, with refinements, a gamma-scaled heuristic of guaranteed relative error 1 - gamma, and a preprocessing rule.
problem_entry: Dynamic programs as column generators for set partitioning LP relaxations; reduce their state space, presented as a rediscovery of DP fathoming (p. 2).
key_idea: Fathom a state when its reduced cost minus the positive duals of elements not yet included is at least min{0, incumbent}; refine with known structure; scale by gamma for a heuristic with a guarantee (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: min c^T x, Ax = 1, x >= 0 with binary A and c >= 0, costs additive along DP transitions (pp. 2-3); valid with convexity constraints, invalid once non-binary columns are allowed (p. 4).
proof_devices: Bound by total relaxation of the extension constraints, then structure added back (maximal set size, incompatible pairs, completion cost) (pp. 3-4)
Lemma 1: scaling the bound by gamma gives relative error at most 1 - gamma, proved by comparing the incumbent with gamma times the bound (p. 4)
Preprocessing: discard an element whose negative dual cannot be made up by all positive duals (p. 4)
Locality: the test needs only the current state, unlike dominance, which needs a global overview (p. 4)
experiments: One sentence: state-space reductions of more than 90% in the locomotive-scheduling application [9]; no table or instance count in the note (p. 4).
positioning: Presents the bound as a rediscovery of DP fathoming (Alekseev and Volodos'; Marsten and Morin; Morin and Marsten), credits Mehrotra and Trick's independent similar bound, and contrasts it with dominance rules (pp. 2, 4).
writing: Four-page note in a modest register (a simple criterion, possibly weak) with one sentence of evidence; referees thanked for readability (pp. 2-5).
limits_future: Bound possibly weak in general; refinements cost effort to weigh against gains; invalid for non-binary columns; heuristic pricing not followed up (pp. 3-4).

method_links.note: Step 6, sole voice: the claim is modest, a simple generic criterion that is possibly weak. Also Heuristic H1, evidence: exact pricing needed at least to prove optimality of the RMP, and the gamma rule turns the exact DP into a heuristic with a known error (pp. 3-4); Taste G1: a heuristic shipped with a proven bound (Lemma 1); Heuristic H4, evidence: a component of his own application code (S054 pp. 7-8) becomes a generic note.
The one performance figure (more than 90%) has no instance set or table behind it in the note.

Strengthen the bound with structure known from the application: maximal route size, incompatible pairs, return cost (pp. 3-4).
Turn an exact pricer into a heuristic with a known guarantee by scaling the bound by gamma (relative error at most 1 - gamma) (p. 4).
Preprocess: drop elements whose negative dual cannot be made up by all positive duals (p. 4).
When an idea has precedents, say rediscovering and cite the independent similar result (pp. 2, 4).

Computational experiments with (2), conducted in the context of a locomotive scheduling problem at in-plant railroads [9], indicate considerable state space reductions of more than 90%.
